title: Activities
text:
What’s missing?
image to come

 What you need
A tray of up to 6 familiar items such as: toothbrush, pen, Duplo block, spoon, ball, play-person. A cloth to cover the tray. Decide on the amount and type of objects according to your knowledge of, and the ages of, the children.


 What to do

Together name each item in turn, whilst placing them on the tray. Without using the cloth, remove and hide one item and ask children if they know which one is missing. Repeat this, with the children taking a turn to remove an item to identify the missing one.
Next time, explain you are going to make the game a little trickier by “secretly” removing one item for them to “work out” which one is missing (avoid the word “guess”), by looking at those that are still there. Cover the tray, secretly remove and hide one item and then uncover the tray for them to see and discuss.



 What to try next

To begin with, you might introduce the game with fewer objects, until they are successful and are keen to make it trickier by increasing the amount.

Children take turns to be the “hider”. Be ready for the ‘joke’ when they remove every one! But, can we name them all?
Ask the children to suggest items to include on the tray.
Try a tray of similar items, e.g. all utensils or all blocks of different shapes. Does this make it trickier? It will depend on the familiarity of and interest in the items. Try 5 different dinosaurs!

Muddle up the objects before uncovering the tray. Does this make a difference to identifying what’s missing?

Play “What’s missing?” with arrangements of counters (subitising) ADD DIAGRAM?, or play “What’s changed?” with a repeating or simple pattern made by the child: “Hide your eyes and I’ll change your pattern – can you spot what I have done?”.



 What to say

Open your eyes and look at the tray …
What do you think is missing? Why do you think that?
Are you sure? How do you know?
What was in that space, do we think?



 What might happen

If a child is unable to identify the missing object, reveal it, and let them work with you, hiding (and naming quietly) an object for other children to identity.
Children might wildly name objects without looking at the tray. If so, using fewer objects and reminding them to look to see what is missing, pointing to the space, might help.



 What matters

“What’s missing?” and “how do we know?” are fruitful mathematical questions that can – and should - be asked in many day-to-day situations where there is a structure or pattern to identify, e.g. laying the table, laying out a correct amount of items, tidying up, and so on. Asking “how do we know?” is an essential part of the activity, where we draw children’s attention to how they think and reason. Whilst we might not always receive an answer, it is an important question to ask. It can be followed, in time, by “Convince me you are right!”.1

It is important we use language like “think” and “work out”, and not “guess”, to draw children’s attention to the fact this is something they can logically puzzle out.



 What to discuss
How are the children responding to our questions: “What’s missing?” and “how do we know?”

title: Activities
text:
Make one like this
image to come

 What you need
Interlocking cubes. NEED image.


 What to do
The adult makes a robot using cubes in one colour only. NEED IMAGE They invite the children to “make one just like this”. Discuss the results together.


 What to try next

Photograph the robots made and leave them out to be discussed and copied.
Show them a peep of the robot and ask them to make one the same. Allow as many peeps as they wish, not allowing them a long look until they are satisfied they are finished and they have made one the same.
Could they draw their robot accurately?
Use squared paper to draw the outline of other simple shapes for children to copy, such as a dog, or a rocket. It is helpful if you use the children’s ideas for these.



 What to say

What will you do first/next/now, I wonder?
What goes there?
Is that it? Is that right?
Which part of the robot is that?
Hmmmm - is that the right number of cubes for the leg?
Is that exactly the same as this? How could you check?
I am going to make a red one exactly the same shape and size as this yellow one!



 What might happen

Children might make their own robots – and indeed other things – especially if the cubes are unfamiliar to them. This is fine, and you might need to return to the challenge of ‘making one exactly the same as this one’. Use this as an opportunity to discuss the decisions they made, the final shape, etc.
You can direct children’s attention to the shape of the robot by drawing your finger around the head, body etc and talking about what you have done.
You might observe children beginning to pay to attention to the size of the robot, for example, the number of cubes they need for the arms or legs, by counting or matching. You can guide them towards accuracy by modelling counting the cubes yourself.



 What matters

Spatial reasoning is crucial for mathematical learning and this activity focuses specifically on the major skill of spatial visualisation.

It is easier for children to copy an actual model, rather than an image of one, as they can handle both, lay one on top of the other, turn these around, etc. Moving between copying models and presenting images of models to copy encourages children to mentally visualise and manipulate images and to represent and interpret two- and three-dimensional objects.

Creating a physical distance between the actual (or image of the) model and children making this (by putting a large-scale ‘poster’ of the model elsewhere or by hiding a model under a cloth allowing only peeps) also supports mental visualisation and interpretation.

Over time, with their attention drawn to both the shapes and amounts in each model, children will become more accurate in making a similar model to one pictured. By providing larger or smaller images of the models to re-create, rather than actual size, you can support children to count, rather than match, the cubes needed in each section.
Using children’s ideas for other models to make or using a model a child has made, will often be more interesting to them, although these might be more complicated! Once the models move away from being ‘flat’, and having depth, these are more difficult to both re-create and to represent.

Sensitive, probing questioning whilst children construct using the cubes, as well as afterwards, reflecting on problem-solving processes and comparing models made, is crucial for supporting children’s spatial and wider mathematical thinking.



 What to discuss

What strategies did our children use to solve this problem?
Which of our questions best allowed us to notice the children’s strategies and to assess and develop their mathematics?

title: Activities
text:
The Bag Game
image to come

 What you need
An opaque (cloth) bag, a tray of pinecones or other similar objects.


 What to do
The children sit in a ring. Show them the empty bag. The bag is passed around the ring with each child adding one pinecone in turn. They count along as each pinecone is added. Before reaching 5 cones in the bag, stop the count, and ask if we know how many cones are in the bag altogether. You may wish to ask how we know. After discussion, tip them out to check. Repeat as many times as they are engaged, starting each time with the empty bag, and when confident, add more than 5 before tipping the bag out to check.


 What to try next

Leave the bag and cones out for the children to re-create the game. Observe them playing with the materials. They may fill the bag with all or as many of the cones as possible.
Revisit the game starting with 6 cones into the bag together. Pass the bag of 6 cones around the ring, with each child removing one cone, counting backwards until the bag is empty.
When the game is known well, this structure can be used to count on. Stop the count at 3, agree there are 3 in the bag without looking, and saying “threeee, slowly add one more, “fourrrr”, pass the bag, “fiveeeee …” etc. Ask how many are in the bag and how we know before tipping out to check as before.
Introduce some recorded music to pass the bag to. Leave the pinecones and bag out. When the music stops, one cone is added to the bag.

Two similar boxes with lids. Count 3 bricks into each box. Move one brick from the first box into the second box. How many are in each box now? Reverse. Repeat.



 What to say

How many are there altogether in the bag? Can you show me using your fingers?
How many are in the bag now? How do we know?
Fin said “Three”, so what does Salim say now?
Together, let’s count back as we take them out.
How many do you think are in the bag now?

Are you sure?
Let’s check!



 What might happen

Children may choose to demonstrate the amount in the bag using their fingers rather than, or as well as, saying the amount. Both finger numbers and the spoken amount are to be encouraged.
Children might be confident adding one at a time up to 5, but not proficient counting backwards. Work on an amount up to and back from 3, then 4.
Children might know the count sequence backwards (or forwards) as a list of counting words, but not attach these words to the actual items.
At first children might not answer your question “How do we know?”, but keep asking this, and leave time for them to think about it.
A child might add 2 cones instead of 1. Treat this as a maths joke! “Ha! TWO more- does anyone know how many are in there now?!”



 What matters

The items can be changed but must be similar in both type and colour, to aid counting of the whole group.
Starting (or ending) with an empty bag is important for experience of the ‘empty set’.
Understanding the cardinality principle involves knowing that the last number you say establishes the quantity of the whole group. Asking “How many are in the bag now?“, and “How many are there altogether in the bag?”, before tipping out the bag to check, draws children’s attention to the last number said.
Counting back is as important as counting forwards, and children will become more confident with counting back as they become familiar with how the game works.



 What to discuss
How did the children surprise us?

title: Activities
text:
Did you know that…
… understanding the directional property of the counting list is a core insight in early number learning?
What is the directional property of the counting list?
Children need to grasp that each number in the counting list represents a quantity that is one more than the one before, and one less than the one after. The “bag game” is useful because it focuses directly on this idea. Children add or remove objects from a bag and have to work out how the total changes.


More…

Unlike many counting activities, where children count objects they can see, this task does not allow them to rely only on pointing and saying number words. In some counting tasks, children can succeed by following a routine of matching each object to a number word without fully understanding how counting works.1,2 In contrast, the bag game requires them to think about how the quantity changes when one item is added or taken away.
The activity can be easily adapted to suit different levels. When small numbers are used (up to three or four), children may be able to keep track of the objects mentally without counting. However, with larger numbers, this is no longer possible. At that point, children need to use their knowledge of counting to work out the new total, moving forwards or backwards in the counting list.3,4
Research shows that even children who can count may not yet understand how numbers change when one is added or removed.5,6 This activity helps to reveal and develop that understanding. Overall, the bag game supports children in moving beyond simply reciting numbers, helping them understand how numbers are ordered and connected.7 This is an important foundation for later arithmetic.

title: Activities
text:
Cutting a square
image to come

 What you need
Paper squares of about 10cm side length in different colours, scissors.


 What to do

Each child selects a paper square. Chat about their choice and ask them what they know about a square. Model and talk through folding your square in half, diagonally, from corner-to-corner.ADD DIAGRAM Ask: What do you see now?
Open your folded square out and re-fold it, several times. Children do the same with their squares and chat about what they are doing.
Everyone cuts their square in half along the diagonal fold to make two triangles. Place the two triangles on top of each other. Ask: Do they fit? Are they the same shape and size as each other? Can children re-make their square from their two triangles? What new shapes can they make by fitting their two triangles together? ADD DIAGRAM
Encourage children to describe what they make, using their own language, whilst you introduce vocabulary such as: similar, different, straight, corner, point, side, edge, touching, half/ halved.
Would children like to choose one of their new shapes to glue onto a poster? Leave out the poster and more paper squares for them to re-create the shapes displayed. Observe children playing with the materials. They may cut the squares into many different pieces!
Revisit the activity, this time folding and cutting the square in half to make two rectangles. Ask: What can we make with these?



 What to try next

Try starting with a different shape and halving this, e.g. a rectangle or a triangle.
Children cut their square into 4 triangles by making a second diagonal fold (“sandwiches”). ADD DIAGRAM This second cut presents many more possibilities. Play with re-arranging the 4 triangles into new shapes and remaking the original square.
Explore tiling (covering / filling) a surface or region with many similar shapes, leaving no spaces; for example, all paper squares or triangles.
Introduce a set of pattern blocks for children to explore. These are related by side-length or angle.ADD DIAGRAM
Visualising what will happen: Sit with a group of children, demonstrate folding a sheet of paper in half, and hovering your scissors where you will make a single cut. ADD DIAGRAM What do they think the piece in your hand will look like when you make the cut and open the new shape out? When modelled clearly, many children enjoy playing with this idea when paper and scissors are left out.



 What to say

What do you think you might be able to make?
How can you describe what you see / what you have made?
Trace your finger all around the edge of your new shape.
Can you repair / remake your square?
I wonder if you could make a shape similar to mine / like hers? Different to ..?

If you place that triangle there, what do you think your new shape will look like?



 What might happen

Some children might need practice folding accurately in half.
They might not be able to resist cutting the square into smaller and smaller pieces!

Children might start by assigning a name to the shapes they make after it is made, like “Roof”, “Rocket”.

It takes time and experience for children to be able to predict what a new arrangement might look like, or to visualise and describe or name something they would like to make (prediction).
Keeping ‘their’ 4 triangles in a named envelope encourages children to revisit this task when they have an idea.



 What matters

Spatial skills can be trained.1 Folding and cutting paper shapes gives children experience of how shapes are composed. Experience of constructing and de-constructing shapes, rather than simply recognising and naming already formed, usually regular, shapes is important. Re-arranging and putting shapes back together is a key way for young children to experience the conservation of area (measures), informally and playfully.

Spatial visualisation and prediction are key to developing children’s mathematical thinking. We can support this by wondering aloud what something might look like and asking questions like “What do you think it might look like if …” or “Can you imagine what it will look like if..?” Whilst children might not have the vocabulary to answer such questions, if we regularly ask these, we are drawing their attention to what matters; ie their thinking processes.
Using gesture is useful in helping children understand vocabulary such as “fold in half”, “under’, “on top” “in front” “beside”, “point”, etc.2
Recognition of what is similar and what is different in a variety of contexts is important mathematically.

title: Activities
text:
My measuring tape
image to come

 What you need
Thin card, paper, ribbon or tape cut into strips of different lengths, with each short enough so that both ends can be held by a child when the tape is stretched to its full length.


 What to do
Choose one tape and play around with measuring it against other tapes. Stretch them out and line up the ends carefully, commenting on what you notice: e.g. Ooo that’s MUCH longer, This one is nearly the same length.
Each interested child is then given their own ‘measuring tape’ to keep and invited to do some measuring. They keep their tape safely to make comparisons for as long as their interest lasts.


 What to try next

Encourage them to use their tape to measure other items, e.g. ask: Will it reach around the tree trunk? If you hold one end on the floor, I wonder if it will reach as high as this chair? Can you find something the same length as your tape?
Children might be interested in experimenting with cutting pieces of string to match the length of different objects.
Leave out a range of tape measures and rulers for children to play with. Put a measuring tape in the role-play area. Retractable tapes are particularly attractive to children and will result in interesting discussions about the numbers!
Look at the rulers – discuss - what are the numbers for? Can children make their own tape-measure or ruler to use?
Compare two tapes and deliberately exaggerate misaligning one end. Say something ridiculous such as, Look how much longer this one is!



 What to say

That is just about (nearly) the same length as yours, I think.
Can you find one that is half as long as your string / that reaches halfway?
Do you think that is (much) shorter than your tape?
Can you find one that is only a little longer (shorter) than yours?
When have you seen someone measuring something? What were they doing?
Are they exactly the same length as each other?
I wonder why we have to make sure we line the ends up carefully?



 What might happen

Every child might say their tape is the longest!
You will notice children comparing their tapes with each other without aligning the ends. Point out that to see how much longer one is than another, we must match up one end carefully. Exaggerate this.
Over time, and with discussion, you might find children attending increasingly to accuracy when comparing lengths.



 What matters

Important early understandings of length are grasping that lengths span a fixed distance, and that comparing lengths accurately requires lining up endpoints carefully. This is the focus of this activity.
There is a lot of specific vocabulary to develop around the different aspects of measure. Rather than relying on “big” or “long”, it is better to focus on the use of “than” and comparative phrases such as “nearly as long as…”, “a lot shorter than…”, “as long as..”



 What to discuss

When and in what context did we notice children attending carefully and accurately making a comparison?
Was there anything that surprised us regarding our children’s understanding of length?

title: Activities
text:
Little Shop
image to come

 What you need
Real 1p coins, purses and wallets.A tray of items to buy, such as small cracker toys.


 What to do
With the children, count up to 8 pennies into each purse or wallet and label the tray of toys “1p shop” or “Penny Stretchers”. Children are invited to choose items to buy from the shop and to check how much is (left) in their purse or wallet by tipping out their coins and counting them back into the purse/wallet, closing the purse and then saying aloud how much they have left to spend.


 What to try next

You might choose to begin with 5 pennies to spend each.
One child could be the shopkeeper and keep count of the shop income!
Leave out the tray of items, purses and coins for more shopping. Introduce pens and clipboards to encourage list-writing.
This activity will also work as a Poundshop using £1 coins.
Play a game with 5 pennies or £1 coins, leaving some visible whilst hiding the rest in a purse for children to work out how many are hidden each time. ADD diagram? Ask children how they are working it out.



 What to say

What will you choose to buy, first? How much do you have in your purse altogether to spend?
How much do you have to spend?
So, how many pennies/much money is left in your purse, now?

How many things have you bought so far?
Do you know how much is left in your purse without counting? How do you know that?

Could you afford to buy any more / two more things?



 What might happen

Children might well need to continually recount what is left in their purse. Try asking if they need to count, or if they know without counting.
As the amount of money in the purse decreases, some children might be able to answer: “How much is left in your purse now?” without counting. This is evidence of understanding of the successor/predecessor function embedded in the count list i.e. knowing which number precedes (and succeeds) another.

Children might use the amount of items they have bought to work out how much money they have spent and then how much they have left to spend.



 What matters

It is important that children count the pennies back into the purse and are then asked when the purse/wallet is closed: “how much/many do you have (left) to spend? Saying aloud how much they have left to spend once the coins are returned to the purse helps children name the whole quantity (cardinality) when this is unseen.
Asking “Do you know how much is left in your purse now?” encourages children to arithmetically reason, without counting.



 What to discuss
What did you notice about the children’s arithmetic confidence?

title: Activities
text:
Did you know that…
…This activity can support the emergence of arithmetic reasoning with concrete quantities? When children reason about how many must be hidden to yield the original total, they are effectively solving a subtraction problem of the form: starting numerosity − visible numerosity = hidden numerosity.


More…

Learning the counting principles and, crucially, understanding the successor/predecessor function embedded in the count list.1 It has been highlighted that successor/predecessor function understanding is tightly linked to children’s ability to coordinate symbolic knowledge (number words) with underlying quantity representations.2
Successful performance reflects not only counting proficiency but also an understanding of how addition and subtraction are inverse operations.3,4 Additionally, when the starting numerosity is fixed at 10, the activity can train number bonds and decomposition-based reasoning to 10.5 This activity is valuable because it can be flexibly adapted to children’s developmental level. With very small sets, it supports early exact quantity representations while, with larger sets, it places increasing demands on counting and cardinal understanding, thereby encouraging the use of counting as a problem-solving tool rather than as a rote procedure.6 It also fosters arithmetic reasoning focusing on the inverse relation between addition and subtraction and potentially promotes number bonds up to 10.
Children are more accurate counting into a container rather than simply moving or touching a row of items, or, importantly, using physical manipulatives rather than abstract/digital objects that cannot be moved or touched.7

title: Activities
text:
Match the dice
image to come

 What you need
A dish and a 1,2,3 spot dice for each player (including yourself), a tray of similar items to use as counters.


 What to do

We make the number of counters match the amount of dots on the dice. Every player starts with 2 counters in their dish.

Decide who starts. They roll their dice and make the number of counters on their plate match the amount shown on the dice. If they roll 3, they collect 1 counter to add to the 2 in their dish, if they roll 1, they remove one of their counters, if they roll a 2, they do nothing! Take it in turns to roll and match their amounts to the dice roll.



 What to try next

Leave out the materials for the children to play.
Replace the dotty dice with a 1,2,3 numeral dice.
Play this large and outdoors with blocks and build towers each time.
Start with a full dish and roll the dice to empty it – try using chocolate box inners as the dishes, in order to see when the tray is full and how many left to empty it.
After children are familiar with the game, invite them to suggest the amount of counters to begin with.



 What to say

I’ve rolled 1 – what do I do now?
2 and now 1 fewer and I am left with 1
You said “3” straight away!
What do you think will happen if … you roll a 3 next time?
Can you tell me what happened that time?
How many dinosaurs are in your dish now? How many when one is taken away/there is one fewer? How do you know that?
What do you want to roll? Why is that?
Do nothing! Why is that?



 What might happen

You might notice children removing the items from their dish each time before counting in the new amount.
Look out for and encourage children to subitise the small amounts each time (without counting each individual counter).
Children might not be able to vocalise what they have done to match the amounts, even if they are successfully solving the problem each time. Encourage them to indicate the changing amounts on their fingers. Often children are more accurate with gesture rather than number word.
As the game becomes familiar, children might be making predictions about what might happen next and even suggest a variation.



 What matters

Similar items, as well as counters, in one colour are necessary to support the children in noticing the amounts and not being distracted by colour or type.
The point is to encourage children to notice connections between the small amounts, eg. 2 and 1 more will be 3 altogether; if I remove 2 I will be left with 1, etc.
It is important that you leave each child time to think themselves how to make the amounts match and not suggest it to them. Cognitive struggle in a safe environment is mathematically highly productive.
Dice choice: Better to begin with a 1,2,3 dotty dice to ensure success and for you to observe their facility managing the game. Introducing a 1,2,3 numeral dice gives children important practice at matching numerals to quantities. Using a 1-6 dice is much more challenging to talk about and will force many children to rely on counting rather than noticing the links between the small amounts. It’s better to move on to a 1-4 dice even though what is rolled is biased.



 What to discuss

What do we notice about children’s addition and subtraction knowledge whilst playing this game? How might we develop this?

title: Activities
text:
Follow Me
image to come

 What you need
Assorted loose parts and shapes, a small mat or card sheet for yourself and each child.


 What to do
You model selecting one loose part at a time placing it on your mat to create a simple symmetrical design or picture. Children watch and “follow me” copying the design, piece by piece. Narrate what you are choosing and where you decide to place each piece e.g. I am going to put one of these shiny beads in each corner, and this pointy shape will be the top of the rocket …
Children can take turns being the leader – this will work best in pairs sitting alongside each other.


 What to try next

Use a cloth to cover your mat and your finished design. Allowing children only glimpses, can they make one exactly the same as yours? Together, enjoy the big reveal when they think they have completed the task. Discuss the similarities and differences.

Try playing “Follow me” with Duplo, large blocks outside or threading beads.
As they become more experienced, you could introduce a small screen between the players, so the follower is listening to the instructions, and only seeing occasional peeps of the design.
Introduce some recorded music to pass the bag to. Leave the pinecones and bag out. When the music stops, one cone is added to the bag.

Try “Follow me” to find some hidden ‘treasure’: One child hides a toy and lays a paper trail for a friend to find it. As they follow the trail, encourage the child to describe where they are going: Straight on, around the chair, it’s under the rug!



 What to say

I am going to make a car. I have found round shapes for wheels but first I am going to put this long rectangle in the middle for the chassis.
Can you follow what I am doing, one piece at a time?

Maybe you could try turning that around to see if it matches this one.
Where will you put that piece, I wonder?
Are you ready for me to do the next part of my picture? Is yours the same so far?

Oooo – stop a minute and check.
What do you notice?
How are they the same/different?
Can you think of a picture for us all to make? Remember to tell us where to put each piece.



 What might happen

Some children will be focussed on choosing and placing each piece and find it hard to say what they are doing as they do it. You could try narrating for them eg I can see you putting the triangle at the top. Encourage them to describe their picture after it is complete.
You will find it useful to use gestures to help children understand the positional vocabulary.
The leader might be so interested in what they are designing that they work too fast for the follower to keep up! Children might need encouragement to keep an eye on what the follower is doing, as well as selecting and placing their own pieces. You might need to stop them and invite them to take a careful check on what is going on.



 What matters

This activity is focussed on recognising and describing spatial orientation and spotting similarities and differences in a shape, pattern or geometric structure.
Firstly, children learn to listen and respond appropriately to the instructional, descriptive and positional vocabulary used by the adult. Keep initial designs simple and make sure the resources used are familiar to the children i.e. they have previously used them freely and extensively.
It is more of a challenge for children to describe what they are doing with sufficient accuracy to create something the same. What is important is that they begin to recognise what they see as “the same” and “different”, and point this out, or correct it.
Be aware that words such as ‘on top’, ‘under’ ,‘beside’ could have several interpretations! This can lead to worthwhile discussions about what these words mean on different situations. NEED image
It is important to be as precise as possible when describing something (children are good word learners) but also to use the informal language which is familiar to children alongside more formal mathematical language.



 What to discuss

How can we connect maths language to what children are currently doing and interested in?
What do we notice about the words the children use themselves when engaged in this activity?

title: Activities
text:
The Box Game
image to come

 What you need
Up to 5 tubs or boxes, with lids, which each hold up to 4 cubes of one colour, pens, sticky notes.


 What to do
Starting with 3 open tubs, together count 1 cube into one tub, 2 cubes into another and 3 cubes into the third tub. Playfully, make sure the children can identify the amount in each tub confidently and correctly, even when the tubs change places.
Next, with the lids on the tubs, can children still point to the tub holding 1 (2, 3)? We might need to look inside – but can we use the pen and a sticky note to label each lid, so we know how many are inside, without looking? The amounts hidden inside the box are labelled by the children.


 What to try next

Change the positions of the labelled tubs. Can we still tell which is which?
Leave tubs, pens, sticky notes and cubes out for children to hide cubes and label. They will probably fill a tub with cubes!
Introduce an empty tub to label (experience of the ‘empty set’) and observe what they decide to do.
Add standard numerals to pen-pots, containers of scissors, paint brushes, and so on, for children to ‘stock take’ at the end of the session.

Calculating a missing amount. Starting with 3 (or 4) cubes, count them together to establish how many there are. Children watch you placing some of these cubes into a box and closing the lid. You indicate the cubes outside the box that can be seen. Then point to the closed box and ask them if they know how many are hidden inside. Develop this into a game, they will be keen to do the hiding themselves.



 What to say

Are you sure this is the tub with 3 inside? How do you know?
How do you know how many are inside, without looking?

Let’s label each one so we don’t have to look inside.
What does this label tell us? I wonder if we will we still know how many are in here, tomorrow?
Where is the empty tub?



 What might happen

Some children will want to use some standard numerals; others will tally or make idiosyncratic marks. What is important is that they are using a mark to signify a quantity.
The empty tub is often interesting, as the lid could be left blank.



 What matters

Playing with cubes of similar size and colour is necessary to help children recognise and name the whole group of 2, 3 etc.
Use cubes or other items that do not obscure one another in the container to encourage subitising.
Children make the decisions about how to label the tubs. Their different ideas, well as standard symbols for 0, 1,2,3,4 etc, can be discussed at a later stage.

Whilst you might not receive an answer to a question such as “How do you know how many are inside, without looking?”, the question is important to ask.



 What to discuss
What opportunities do our children have to write, as well as to read, symbols linked to quantities?

text:
Fitting it in
image to come

 What you need
Shape-sorting boxes, or inset jigsaws NEED IMAGE


 What to do
Arrange the puzzle pieces on the floor or a low table and sit alongside. If there is more than one jigsaw available and the pieces are mixed, this is much more challenging. Children are encouraged to complete the puzzle with the adult narrating, using vocabulary alongside appropriate hand gestures, such as: twist, turn it around, fit, straight, curved, smaller, bigger.


 What to try next

Cut the front of a familiar cereal box into 4 to make a homemade jigsaw.
Hide a shape from a shape-sorter to see if they can spot which is missing.
Collect nesting items of different shapes to play with, order, stack and fit together, such as stacking cups in a stacking-cup set, or nesting dolls.

Cut different sized holes in the lid of a plastic container to post things into or post balls down different sizes of cardboard tube.
Linked activities that are related to spatial visualisation involve physical movement and navigation (see the activity ‘Maps’). For example: working with children to create simple roads and rail tracks and talking about position, e.g. I wonder which way will the track turn now? “Shall we put this bridge next to the house or the river? or navigating around your environment Can you remember what we saw in between the shop and the bus stop? NEED IMAGE



 What to say

Do you think this is the piece that might fit here? (Holding or indicating an incorrect as well as a correct piece.)
What if you turn that all the way around/over?

I wonder why this won’t fit?
I think I am going to try flipping this one over to see if it fits.



 What might happen

Children might try one shape/piece and discard this when it doesn’t fit straight away. They may need encouragement to try turning the same piece to check if it fits.

When playing, talk about the shape of the pieces you are selecting and why. Use I wonder if… Children might not appear to be listening, but this models our thinking.



 What matters

Relaxed adult attendance and narration is an important way to interest children in persisting to solve puzzles, as well as to introduce them to spatial vocabulary. As you play together, use both informal language such as flat, round, curvy, twist, pointy; and more formal language such as square, straight, corner, rotate, flip.
Appropriate gestures help children understand new vocabulary.
Asking thoughtful questions such as: Do you think that…? and What if you try … encourages mental prediction and manipulation, both of which are central aspects of spatial awareness.



 What to discuss

Which comments or questions most helped children to solve the puzzles?
How might we organise our jigsaws and puzzles so that they remain of sufficient interest and challenge to the children?

title: Activities
text:
Blocks and Stories
image to come

 What you need
Wooden building blocks of a variety of shapes and sizes. Flat floor space within which to build as well as uninterrupted time to do so, including leaving the creations out on display, both complete and incomplete.
Images of buildings, eg castles, towers, bridges etc. NEED IMAGE
A vertical flat surface nearby to display photographs of creations and other construction images.


 What to do

Play alongside children, either building your own construction or building collaboratively. Commentate what you are doing and why you are selecting a particular block, eg: I think this sloping shape might make a good roof.
Displaying both the constructions themselves and collecting photographs of the built and partially built structures values the block play and provides opportunities to develop what is taking place over time. For example, when appropriate you could introduce a story context with a problem to solve, e.g. a bridge for a lorry to make a delivery to the castle, or a house big enough for a toy elephant.



 What to try next

Introduce a familiar story to the block area.
When appropriate, add clipboards and pens for children to draw their creations.
Take photographs of the building to make into a floor book, which will demonstrate developing spatial awareness and creativity over time.
Take construction outside by providing items to build with e.g. blocks, planks, tyres, crates, log-slices etc.



 What to say

This block is too short to stretch across here. I need a longer one that’s just the same shape.
I need two blocks the same height to make my bridge.
I wonder if this block is flat enough to stand up by itself?

I wonder … what shall we build today?
Oooo, what shapes do we need to make an arch?



 What might happen

Young children begin by enjoying knocking down towers built by adults, and progress to adding blocks to towers built collaboratively. Next, come lines of blocks to make ‘roads’ and gradually walls, bridges and enclosures. All are important stages of thinking and getting to know the properties of different shapes of block.
As children become more experienced, you will see them begin to select blocks for a specific purpose and reject others, e.g. blocks of the same shape to make a road. This is an indication that they are visualising what they want to create.

You also might recognise aspects of symmetry – or ‘balance’ - in what they create. Draw their attention to this.


 What matters

The most important thing is time and space. Time is necessary for the children to get fully involved and gradually learn to collaborate with others creating structures and buildings they can play with.

Talking together with adults about the children’s creations after the play has finished gives children the distance to think and talk about what they have been involved in, and for the adult to introduce vocabulary to describe the structures. Time after the play provides reflection time for the children, and opportunities for them to discuss developments and improvements as well as for the adult to provide further stimulus.
Unit blocks are the ideal resource, i.e. those related to each other in size and shape, so that two of these make one of these (ADD IMAGE). Also providing a wide range of materials for construction indoors and outdoors is important, including a range of recycled materials which provide real life examples of shapes e.g. kitchen roll tubes, tissue boxes, party hats, tyres, etc.



 What to discuss

How did your children surprise you?
Did you notice children selecting particular blocks, shapes or lengths for specific purpose they had in mind?

title: Activities
text:
The Bag Game
image to come

 What you need
Strips of card with a strip of double-sided tape end to end, pens.


 What to do

Children take the prepared card strips and a pen out for a short walk, chatting together as you walk about where you are going and what you see. As you pass a ‘landmark’, such as a post box, a gate, or you make a turn, children pick something up or make a mark on their strip to remind them where they went, what they passed and in which order.
Back home, they are invited to use their card strips to talk through their walk.



 What to try next

Can we collaboratively create maps of our walk on large paper sheets?
Children create their maps of the setting to show their families where their favourite places to play and favourite things are positioned.
Create an obstacle course and then invite children to draw maps of this. Using open-ended materials outdoors that can be transported offers opportunities for children to build and discuss maps of their surroundings. NEED image
Making sense together of other visual images such as photographs (Where is this, I wonder?) and diagrams, such as those accompanying construction materials (I wonder if we can make this?).



 What to say

What are you noticing?
Will you include that on your map?
What will you do to remember that?
Can you remember what we walked past just after the school gate?

I wonder, did we turn left at the end of the path?
Ooo, I notice you have included the swings – did I do that too?
Then what did you see? What came next?
Can you point to the shop on your map?
I’m going to talk through my journey – make sure I remember everything!



 What might happen

It is important children are given opportunities to represent both simple journeys and familiar environments as maps. These will be linear to begin with, relative distances and more complex positions emerging later, and with experience.
Children’s ‘maps’ of their journeys are unlikely to match each other’s (or ours!), as they remember different things or consider different moments as important landmarks. These differences present opportunities for discussion and the inclusion of further landmarks.
As they move to drawing a map, whilst the resulting images might match their walk in places, they might recreate a much wider familiar environment in their post-drawn maps.



 What matters

Spatial reasoning is crucial for mathematical learning and this activity focuses specifically on the major skill of spatial orientation.

Children’s understanding of maps and their navigation abilities develop slowly, becoming more sophisticated only in the later primary years. Maps – both looking at them and creating them - supports the development of children’s navigation abilities by giving them opportunities to think and talk about spatial relationships between places in environments that are familiar to them.
Initially we can focus on the sequencing of landmarks they notice, which links to their sequencing more generally, for example when understanding time.



 What to discuss

Which children surprised us by their interest in map-making, or by their abilities in accurately re-creating a journey?
How could we further develop these interests?

title: Activities
text:
NUmbers on a line
image to come

 What you need
Outdoor chalks, large 0-5 dotty dice (i.e. one face is blank, with no dots)


 What to do
Children roll the dice, count - or subitise - the dots and then chalk the correct numeral on the ground. When you think it appropriate, introduce the idea of chalking the numbers in order along a horizontal line, from zero.


 What to try next

Jumping onto a digit when a number is rolled.
Jumping along the line of numbers saying each number in turn, up and back. Can we make up a game to play on our line of numbers?
Can they continue the line above 5?
Use a 0,1,2 dice to jump along the line of numbers, starting from zero. When you roll zero, you don’t move.
Take it in turns to secretly stand on – and hide - a number on the line for others to identify which number is hidden.
Build a ‘How old are you?’ number line together, with children, relatives and friends positioned on it. Include zero. Do we know anyone who is zero? What does that mean?
Count aloud in unison up from zero (stop at different numbers as experiences develop) and back again. Slap your knees or stamp in a steady rhythm as you count.



 What to say

You’ve rolled (…). What number shall we write?
It’s blank! Nothing! Can we write something for nothing?
When I say “go” jump on …

Can we jump on the numbers in order?
Let’s write them all in order along this line, starting with zero
What comes next/after 3? Are you sure?



 What might happen

Toddlers have practical experience of zero, usually when things have “all gone”, or “nothing left”, this activity introduces ‘nothingness’ and ‘doing nothing’. Some children might insist on rolling the dice again to get a number of dots.

Some children might know the symbol for zero, whilst others might be meeting this for the first time. Ask children where they have seen it before and what it might mean.
Writing the 0-5 numerals in order on a horizontal line might be challenging enough for some. It is far more challenging to roll the dice to produce each number randomly, as children have to decide where to position the rolled number each time, allowing for numbers not yet there.
The numbers might not be evenly spaced, which at this early stage is fine as we are focussing on ordering numerals in sequence.
Children might reverse numerals when writing them. As age-appropriate, you can correct this sensitively without stunting children’s enthusiasm.



 What matters

Here, we are building young children’s number sense through playing with and creating simple number lines – usually a horizontal line on which equally spaced points are given numbers, and including zero. This is a spatial model of number. This is not the same thing as children using printed number lines, which is difficult for young children.
Children think about zero in different ways, as an endpoint (“5,4,3,2,1, ZERO!”), or as an absence of something (see activity ‘Same and Different’). Zero may well play a special role in children’s numerical understanding, as they come to learn that it ‘behaves’ in exceptional ways.
Building a mental number line – an ordered list of numerals - with increasing sophistication as children become older, is as important for their mathematical development as their experiences of numbers as amounts. Number line understanding contributes to understandings of number relationships, estimation and calculation.

Ordering numbers is the process of working out which number is larger than or smaller than another. Ordinal number knowledge is not just about the quite complex ordinal language of “first” “second” “third”… and so on, but also to do with how each number relates to another in the sequence of counting numbers.
Playing simple board (track) games can develop children’s ordinal understanding.



 What to discuss

Are there any surprises as children engage in this activity?
How did different children respond when ordering the numerals?

title: Activities
text:
Listen and Count
image to come

 What you need
A container such as an empty tin and some penny coins, or counters that make a noise when dropped into the tin.


 What to do
Children listen to a small number of counters being dropped one-by-one into the tin. When you stop, they say how many counters, or hold up a number of fingers, to show how many they think are in the tin altogether, before tipping them out and counting by sight.


 What to try next

Children close their eyes as you drop in the counters, only opening them when you finish each time.
Leave out tins and counters for children to play with the idea of listening and counting.
Experiment dropping the counters in a regular rhythm, and then irregularly. Can children still keep accurate count?

Give each child a plate and counters. They place one of their counters onto their plate every time they hear a counter drop into the tin. Does the number on their plate match the number in the tin each time?

Count the beats of a drum.

Experiment hiding small numbers of coins into different tins and shaking the tins to estimate how many are inside before looking and checking.



 What to say

Listen carefully and count how many sounds you hear.
Show me with your fingers how many you heard altogether.
How many do YOU think are in the tin this time? Can you explain why?
Try to count every penny as you hear it drop into the tin. How many times did I drop in a counter?
Five is what you heard, so how many do you think we will see when we tip them out?
How sure are you?
Were we right this time? Why/why not?
You tip them out and arrange them so we can easily see how many there are.



 What might happen

To begin with, keep the amount dropped to 5 and under and watch and listen out for children able to accurately keep count of the amount, even when you drop the coins in an uneven rhythm. These children might not be able to name the overall amount in the tin (the cardinal principal) without more experience.

Sometimes the coin bounces and creates two noises. This leads to interesting discussions when the tin is emptied.



 What matters

It is important that children experience success and show interest in this counting activity, in order they are willing to repeat – and practise – counting in many different contexts. Thus, it is necessary to keep the amounts small.

The items can be changed but must be similar in both type and colour to aid identification of the final amount as one group.
When children play with the idea themselves, they are likely to explore extremes, by dropping large numbers – or handfuls - of counters into the tin which they then find difficult to count both by ear and visually! This is fine and fun for them to explore and you to enjoy with them: Why can’t we see how many that is? Wow! That’s LOADS! It’s probably a million!
Some children might hold up one finger each time they hear a sound. This is something to encourage if someone appears to be struggling to keep count.
It is more difficult to count the number of beats, say on a drum, as there is nothing to check as there is for this activity.



 What to discuss

Which of our children demonstrated numerical curiosity during this activity, maybe by making a comment or asking a question?

What different counting opportunities and contexts can we develop for our children?

title: Activities
text:
Same and different
image to come

 What you need
Six identical containers, each large enough to cover small quantities of pebbles, or similar objects.


 What to do
Using the 6 containers, with the children, cover 1, 2 and 3 pebbles so that there are two containers covering each amount. Playfully lift each container and invite comment on how many are underneath. With all objects covered, move the containers about. Children choose two containers to lift to see if they each cover the same amount.


 What to try next

Include two more containers with nothing underneath. Can we find two containers covering zero pebbles?
Introduce a puppet who makes mistakes, for example saying the amounts match when they do not, or calling out ‘Three!’ when the amount is two. Can children notice and correct their mistakes?

Children ‘win’ the two amounts if they match. Compare winnings.
Model wondering how many pebbles you can hold in your hand. Ask, How about you? Is that more or fewer do you think?
Leave the cups and the pebbles for the children to play with the idea. You could try including numeral cards for children to match symbols to quantities.
Using only 5 (or fewer) pebbles each time, arrange each group of 5 into a pattern e.g. diagonal line, a dice-5, etc. Make and cover two of each arrangement. Children choose two covers to lift up and talk about what they see, asking What is the same? What is different?



 What to say

I wonder if we can find two cups with the same amount underneath.
Have you found two amounts the same? No?!

Which cup is covering more (fewer) pebbles? How do you know?
What do you see? Ooo, show me with your fingers what’s under each cup.
How do you know these are the same?

Are they both three? Is that right?



 What might happen

Some children might need encouragement to pay attention to the amount under each cup. Others might have to touch or move the pebbles under each to check the amounts match.
“Fewer” is the correct word to use in this context as we are comparing discrete quantities, whereas “less” applies to continuous quantity such as length and time, but children might be more familiar “less” than with “fewer” and you might need to use both words and use a gesture to accompany “fewer”.

If children make mistakes recognising the amounts, reduce the amounts to 0 – 2, and/or model making a mistake yourself matching or naming the amounts for them to spot: Watch me/listen to me carefully!



 What matters

The main object of this activity is to compare two quantities to see if they are the same, or whether one group has more or fewer than the other. Rather than exclaiming yourself when two identical cups are found, encourage children to say what they see when they lift the cups each time.
Recognising small amounts, for example by encouraging subitising, supports children in learning to link quantities to number words and marks the beginnings of cardinal understanding (where a number stands for a group of objects).
Recognising different arrangements but of the same quantity (e.g. all 4s) deepens children’s cardinal number knowledge.



 What to discuss

What is there to notice about different children’s confidence and facility in recognising and matching small amounts?
Were there any examples of children explaining what they notice?

title: Activities
text:
Water Play
image to come

 What you need
Transparent containers to fill of a range of sizes, shapes, heights and widths, access to coloured water and a flat surface on which to stand the filled containers.


 What to do
Whilst – or after - children play freely with the water and containers, choose one container that is tall and thin and another that is short and wide, and together discuss their shapes and sizes. Notice children using gestures as well as language, for example, children might indicate the narrowness of a container with their hands or fingers whilst talking about its height. Compare the shapes of some different containers. Ask children to choose one or two to talk about, if you hold them up, they are free to use gesture as well as language.


 What to try next

Fill a taller container and pour this into a shorter one, asking which container they think holds the most water.
Tell children you are going to secretly choose a container and show it to them quickly. Say, You’ll get to peep – and then you tell me what you quickly noticed about the shape and size. Do you want another peep? And another?

With the children, mark a horizontal line on similar containers, either near the top, around halfway down, or nearer the bottom. If not using an indelible pen, a horizontal band of masking tape operates well as an ‘up-to’ line. Explain this is an ‘up-to’ line to fill up to, no more, no less. Can they pour carefully and then compare how much water is in each one? IMAGE REQUIRED



 What to say

This one looks taller, I wonder if it might hold more? Hmmm, what about how fat it is?
What do you notice about this container?

Tell me why you have chosen this one.
Let’s find the one that holds the most (least) water!

Ooo, I’m having to put more water in this one to fill up this one to the brim!



 What might happen

Children might not be interested in talking about the containers. Try having a chat after their water play has finished or take photos to talk about later.
Children might appear to be focussed on the height of a container rather than any other attribute. Gradually, with encouragement, they might begin to use gesture to indicate the width of a container.



 What matters

To focus attention on the mathematics, select the containers carefully, and change them often. Transparency as well as using coloured water ensures the liquid level is as visible as possible. Make sure you include at least one or two containers that are tall and thin and have less capacity than shorter, fatter ones. And make sure the children can lift the full containers as well as being able to reach to pour into the containers’ necks with care.
Discussing photographs of their play will help children become more aware of their thinking and provide opportunities for you to stimulate and develop their thinking.



 What to discuss

If we focus on children’s language use alone, are we missing opportunities to capitalize on what these children understand? How do we consciously and deliberately introduce gesture into our mathematical moments?
How did the different children respond to comparing different containers and how has this helped their understanding of capacity?

text:
The Three Bears
image to come

 What you need
The picturebook of The Three Bears and a collection of different lengths of rod - Cuisenaire rods are ideal (image & reference here?).


 What to do
Read and enjoy the story with the children. Before the second reading, invite them to each choose one rod to represent Daddy bear, one rod for Mummy bear and one for Baby bear. Allow them sufficient time to chat, choose, and to change their minds if they wish.
Now re-tell the story (slowly!) and when the children hear “Daddy Bear” they each hold up their Daddy Bear rods, on hearing “Mummy Bear” they hold up their Mummy Bear rods, and likewise for Baby Bear.


 What to try next

Children hide their three Bears behind their backs to identify by feel alone.
Children lay out their rods/Bears lining up the end points carefully to look at different and similar choices and invite children to explain their decisions.They say what they notice about the different rods chosen and the differing lengths of rod.
Add challenge by reducing the range of rods to choose from, eg, the first five, as this would lead to finer comparisons being made, especially by feel alone.

OTHERS FROM JUNE VERSION? * Leave out the rods and the picture book for children to recreate the activity, telling the story themselves. * Invite children to draw long, short and middle-sized rods, sticks , people or bears. Encourage the use of a baseline to line up the endpoints. * Outdoors ask children to find a tall, middle sized and short stick. * Can they order a larger stick collection from longest to shortest? * Introduce a set of nesting cups or toys for children to explore and organise by size.


 What to say

Can you tell us about your bear family - which bear is which? Can you describe how long each rod is?
Let’s line up your bears carefully to see how much taller/longer Daddy is than Baby.
Do you see anyone with the same rods as you have chosen? How can you be sure (prove) these are same length as each other?
Which is your middle-sized rod/bear? Can you show me?
How do you know which rod is which without looking?

OTHERS FROM JUNE VERSION? * That’s a different Mummy bear rod, isn’t it? I wonder why? * This is longer than/ taller than, this one, and this one is shorter than these….


 What might happen

Children might spot others who have chosen the same rods as them, as well as comment when a different rod is held up to their own. Encourage them to explain why they made their choice, and other choices they might have made.
Children might need encouragement to align the ends of their rods.

When selecting rods by feel alone, children might check visually before holding up the rod.
They might want to choose a rod for Goldilocks. This will lead to interesting discussions about what they choose and how the length of this rod relates to their others. Remember it was Baby Bear’s bowl/chair/bed that were the correct size!



 What matters

Comparisons are critical to learning about length, as well as to mathematics more generally. Something is only ‘long’ when compared to something that is shorter, ‘small’ in relation to something bigger.
Children benefit from a wide variety of experiences comparing the length of objects and learning to line up the end points to make accurate comparisons. The latter can be emphasised in this activity.
Discussions are important about who has chosen which rod, and why, to stand for each bear, as well as spotting similarities and differences between choices.

OTHERS FROM JUNE VERSION? * More than three lengths of rod are needed for children to choose from, in order they make decisions about what they see as long, short and middle sized. * Opportunities for children to make length comparisons and to develop their understanding of the language of measure, from big and small to using comparative language such as: middle sized, long (er than), tall (er than), short (er than), about as long as…, much shorter than…, (about) the same length as… etc.


 What to discuss

What other opportunities do we have for children to compare lengths (and widths)?
What are we drawing our children’s attention to? How do we emphasize length as a distance between endpoints rather than as ‘one end sticking out’?
